source.title: Understanding the Interaction of Adversarial Training with Noisy Labels
source.authors: Jia-Ning Zhu; Jing-Feng Zhang; Bo Han; Tong-Liang Liu; Gang Niu; Hong-Xia Yang; Mohan Kankanhalli; Masashi Sugiyama

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Reports natural test accuracy under label noise, extending generalization results to adversarial training with noisy labels. It does not test the listed claim versions directly.
record.gate_note: The paper compares standard training (ST) and adversarial training (AT) with noisy labels, including natural test accuracy. These results concern a setting not covered by the listed versions; no random-label capacity, width, architecture comparison, optimizer comparison, batch-size sweep, dropout intervention, magnitude-aware sharpness measure, or memorized-example removal test is reported. Values shown only in accuracy figures are recorded as figure only. Cited findings from other papers are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures adversarial training's effects on memorization and natural test accuracy under partial label corruption. It does not test any listed version: V1 requires the natural-label versus fixed random-label comparison, and V7 requires magnitude-aware weight perturbations and generalization-gap rankings. The other versions' interventions are absent.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that AT's smoothing reduces memorization of incorrect labels and helps distinguish correct from incorrect examples. They propose PGD-step geometry values for distinguishing correct/incorrect and typical/rare data, and demonstrate robust annotation and annotation-confidence applications.
record.recipe_differences: Studies adversarial training under noisy labels and compares it with standard training; it does not reproduce the natural-label versus random-label experiments central to the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset (CIFAR-10 versus MNIST), noise type (symmetric-flipping versus pair-flipping), and noise rate affect the reported outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Across the reported noise types and rates, AT reduces the late-training deterioration in natural test accuracy associated with ST. Noise still hurts CIFAR-10 accuracy; on MNIST, AT approaches noise-free performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial training can mitigate natural-test-accuracy degradation from partial label corruption, depending on the dataset and noise conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 5 depicts the AT loss landscape as smoother and flatter than the ST landscape on CIFAR-10 with 20% symmetric noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial training under label noise can yield qualitatively flatter visualized loss landscapes alongside reduced test-accuracy deterioration.

record.problems: Natural test-accuracy values are presented in figures without stated numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The study examines noisy-label training, so it does not directly test the listed claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version rows identified. Other plotted results on training accuracy, entropy, loss, and geometry value concern distinguishing correct from incorrect training examples or smoothing under noisy labels, rather than the listed versions' measures.

untested.parts: No comparison of near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels with natural-label generalization and chance-level random-label test accuracy. Corruption rates are only 0.1–0.4, and image experiments use weight decay and CIFAR-10 augmentation.
No width sweep beyond the width needed for zero training error; the ResNet comparison varies depth.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classification comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
No controlled adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets.

Figure 5 offers qualitative loss-landscape visualizations, without the specified magnitude-aware sharpness measure, similarly low training-loss comparison, or rankings against norm and margin measures.
No influence-based memorization measurement followed by removal and retraining against random-removal controls.

record.verdict_notes: Related generalization results do not make this a T3 test of a listed version. The corrected cannot_determine states indicate that the rows cannot establish those versions, not that the authors' qualitative mitigation finding is unreadable.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare fitting random labels with generalization on natural labels, or report held-out accuracy on random labels.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or comparison with other generalization measures.
Does not remove memorized examples and retrain to measure test accuracy.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Standard training on CIFAR-10 with symmetric-flipping label noise; natural test accuracy measured across epochs.
rows.note: The text says ST test accuracy drops more seriously in later training as noise rate increases; exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: No listed version is measured. Figure 17(a) also includes a zero-noise control, which should replace the unspecified baseline; exact curve values cannot be recovered from the supplied text.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Adversarial training on CIFAR-10 with symmetric-flipping label noise; natural test accuracy measured across epochs.
rows.note: The authors state AT alleviates label-noise effects; larger noise lowers AT accuracy, but overfitting is not obvious.
rows.check: The reported mitigation is outside the listed versions, so observed is not a claim-version state. Distinguish the ST comparison from the AT zero-noise control in Figure 17(a).
